name: Ariel Tabak Outside Passing System
description: Study outside guard passing with a focused Ariel Tabak course match, practical partner drills, clear decisions, and ways to review your progress.
summary: The Ariel Tabak Outside Passing System connects movement beyond the defender's legs to upper-body control, using side changes, leg traps, and north-south routes when the guard recovers.
overview:
Getting around the feet is often only the start of an outside pass. A defender can turn, pummel a leg back inside, or frame on the upper body before control settles. This study plan separates the initial flank from the finish so you can see which part of the exchange actually needs work.

Outside Passing Compendium by Ariel Tabak is the matched instructional. Tabak covers outside-leg access, upper-body connection, high-pummel responses, leg-trap finishes, and cross-grip passing. The drills, sequence, and assessment criteria below are an original BJJGraph study plan; use them to organize practice alongside the course and feedback from a coach.
key_principles: Distinguish getting outside the legs from controlling the torso.
Recognize a returning leg before settling your weight.
Use a side change to solve a problem rather than to move aimlessly.
Keep the selected grip arrangement consistent during early drills.
Observe where the defender's shoulders remain free to turn.

key_components.description: Start against a supine guard and aim only to get outside the legs while the defender tries to square up.
key_components.purpose: Separate reaching an angle from securing a pass.

key_components.description: Begin from an established flank and work toward a defined chest or shoulder control while the defender frames.
key_components.purpose: Find the missing link between angle and control.

key_components.description: Let the defender pummel one leg back between the bodies and rehearse a reviewed continuation or side change.
key_components.purpose: Account for the most immediate guard recovery.

key_components.description: Choose one leg-trap grip arrangement and test a single finish before adding alternative grips or routes.
key_components.purpose: Make a broad passing catalog into a manageable branch.

common_obstacles.obstacle: You circle around the feet but never settle control.
common_obstacles.solution: Start already flanked and isolate the upper-body connection.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The defender replaces a high leg during every finish.
common_obstacles.solution: Give the defender that single recovery option and review a matching continuation.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Constant side changes produce motion without progress.
common_obstacles.solution: Define the cue that justifies changing sides and pause when it is absent.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Leg-trap practice mixes several incompatible grips.
common_obstacles.solution: Choose one grip configuration and one finish for the first set of rounds.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: BJJGraph practice suggestion: Start against a supine guard and aim only to get outside the legs while the defender tries to square up. Then connect it to upper-body connection. Compare the first lost control point after each round. Keep the first repetitions cooperative and agree on resistance, space, and reset conditions. Once the starting task is clear, add one defensive option at a time and compare the result with the intended control objective.

flashcards.question: Why is getting outside the feet insufficient to finish a pass?
flashcards.answer: The defender may still turn, frame, or replace a leg before you establish control of the upper body.

flashcards.question: How can you isolate a weak outside-passing finish?
flashcards.answer: Begin from an already flanked position and let the defender frame while you work toward one defined upper-body connection.

flashcards.question: What should trigger a side change in practice?
flashcards.answer: A specific obstruction or recovery should justify the side change, so you can explain how the movement improves the route.

flashcards.question: What is a useful first recovery task for the defender?
flashcards.answer: Allow one high leg to pummel back inside so the passer can study that problem without every guard option at once.

flashcards.question: Why keep one leg-trap grip arrangement during early practice?
flashcards.answer: Consistent grips make it easier to identify whether the problem is the trap, the angle, or the selected finish.

flashcards.question: What gi-specific limitation should a no-gi student recognize?
flashcards.answer: Parts of the course use collar, sleeve, and trouser grips, so those sequences need separate consideration before no-gi practice.
